title: KV Cache and Speculative Decoding
summary: This day covers essential concepts for building AI engineering skills.
content:
# KV Cache and Speculative Decoding ##### The 2,400-token system prompt paid for 40,000 times a day A support automation team in Chennai had a carefully engineered system prompt: role definition, tone rules, twelve few-shot examples, an escalation policy, and a formatted product catalogue. 2,400 tokens. It worked well. It was also identical on every single request, and they served 40,000 requests a day. Every request re-processed those 2,400 tokens through all 32 transformer layers to produce KV cache entries that were bit-for-bit identical to the previous request's. 96 million tokens of prefill per day computing the same thing. Enabling prefix caching took one flag. Time to first token dropped from 890ms to 140ms. Prefill compute dropped by 84%. Their GPU count went from four to two. **The KV cache is the largest lever in inference optimisation after batching** — it dominates memory, it dominates decode bandwidth, and the parts of it that repeat are free to reuse. Day 31 covered PagedAttention; today is caching, quantization, and speculative decoding. ##### KV cache mechanics During decode, attention needs the keys and values for every previous token. Recomputing them each step is O(n²); caching makes it O(n). $$\text{KV bytes} = 2 \times L \times n_{kv} \times d_{head} \times \text{dtype} \times \text{seq\_len} \times \text{batch}$$ ```python def kv_cache_size(n_layers, n_kv_heads, head_dim, seq_len, batch=1, dtype_bytes=2): per_token = 2 * n_layers * n_kv_heads * head_dim * dtype_bytes return { "bytes_per_token": per_token, "kb_per_token": round(per_token / 1024, 1), "total_gb": round(per_token * seq_len * batch / 1e9, 2), } MODELS = { "Llama-3-8B (GQA 8)": dict(n_layers=32, n_kv_heads=8, head_dim=128), "Llama-3-70B (GQA 8)": dict(n_layers=80, n_kv_heads=8, head_dim=128), "Mistral-7B (GQA 8)": dict(n_layers=32, n_kv_heads=8, head_dim=128), "GPT-3-175B (MHA 96)": dict(n_layers=96, n_kv_heads=96, head_dim=128), } for name, cfg in MODELS.items(): r = kv_cache_size(**cfg, seq_len=8192, batch=32) print(f"{name:24s} {r['kb_per_token']:>6.1f} KB/token " f"{r['total_gb']:>7.1f} GB @ 8k×32") # Llama-3-8B (GQA 8) 128.0 KB/token 34.4 GB @ 8k×32 # Llama-3-70B (GQA 8) 320.0 KB/token 85.9 GB @ 8k×32 # GPT-3-175B (MHA 96) 4608.0 KB/token 1237.9 GB @ 8k×32 ``` **The GPT-3 row is why GQA exists.** 1.2 TB of KV cache for a batch of 32 is not servable on any hardware; the Day 2 shift to grouped-query attention was driven by exactly this arithmetic. **Two things scale the cache:** sequence length linearly, and batch size linearly. Since you want large batches for throughput (Day 31) and long context for capability, the cache becomes the binding constraint on both. ```python def max_concurrency(gpu_gb, model_gb, n_layers, n_kv_heads, head_dim, avg_seq_len, dtype_bytes=2, overhead_gb=2.0): """How many concurrent sequences fit after weights and overhead?""" kv_budget = (gpu_gb - model_gb - overhead_gb) * 1e9 per_seq = 2 * n_layers * n_kv_heads * head_dim * dtype_bytes * avg_seq_len return {"kv_budget_gb": round(kv_budget / 1e9, 1), "gb_per_sequence": round(per_seq / 1e9, 3), "max_concurrent": int(kv_budget / per_seq)} print(max_concurrency(80, 16, 32, 8, 128, 4096)) # {'kv_budget_gb': 62.0, 'gb_per_sequence': 0.537, 'max_concurrent': 115} ``` That `max_concurrent` number is the ceiling on your `max_num_seqs` from Day 31 — set it higher and vLLM will preempt and swap, which costs latency. ##### Prefix caching The Chennai fix. If two requests share a prefix, the KV entries for that prefix are identical and can be reused. ```mermaid flowchart TD A["Request 1:
[system 2400 tok][user A 40 tok]"] --> B["Prefill all 2440"] B --> C[("Cache blocks
for system prefix")] D["Request 2:
[system 2400 tok][user B 55 tok]"] --> E{"Prefix match?"} C --> E E -->|"2400 tokens hit"| F["Prefill only 55 new tokens"] F --> G["TTFT: 890ms → 140ms"] ``` ```bash # vLLM --enable-prefix-caching # SGLang uses RadixAttention — a radix tree over prefixes, better for # branching conversations and agent trees python -m sglang.launch_server --model-path ... --enable-flashinfer ``` **Structure your prompts so the stable part comes first.** This is the same principle as provider prompt caching from Day 42's beginner article, and it applies identically to self-hosted serving: ```python def build_cacheable_prompt(system, few_shots, retrieved_chunks, user_query): """Stable prefix first, variable content last — maximises cache hits.""" return [ {"role": "system", "content": system}, # identical every request *few_shots, # identical every request {"role": "user", "content": # varies f"Context:\n{retrieved_chunks}\n\nQuestion: {user_query}"}, ] ``` **A common mistake that destroys cache hits:** putting a timestamp, request ID, or the user's name at the *start* of the system prompt. One varying token at position 3 invalidates the entire 2,400-token prefix. Put variable content at the end, always. **Provider prompt caching** works the same way with different economics: | Provider | Discount on cached prefix | Minimum prefix | TTL | |---|---|---|---| | Anthropic | 90% cheaper reads | 1024 tokens | 5 min (refreshable) | | OpenAI | 50% cheaper | 1024 tokens | 5–60 min, automatic | | Self-hosted (vLLM) | 100% — no recompute | 1 block (16 tokens) | Until evicted | ```python # Anthropic explicit cache control response = client.messages.create( model="claude-3-5-sonnet-20241022", system=[ {"type": "text", "text": LONG_SYSTEM_PROMPT, "cache_control": {"type": "ephemeral"}}, # ← mark as cacheable ], messages=[{"role": "user", "content": query}], max_tokens=1024, ) print(response.usage.cache_read_input_tokens) # verify the hit ``` **Verify your hit rate.** `cache_read_input_tokens` near zero when you expected a hit means your prefix is not actually stable — go find the varying token. ##### KV cache quantization The cache is the memory bottleneck; quantizing it buys concurrency directly. ```python def kv_quantization_benefit(n_layers, n_kv_heads, head_dim, seq_len, gpu_kv_gb=60): """Concurrency gain from lower-precision KV cache.""" rows = [] for name, bytes_per in [("fp16", 2), ("fp8", 1), ("int8", 1), ("int4", 0.5)]: per_seq = 2 * n_layers * n_kv_heads * head_dim * bytes_per * seq_len rows.append({ "dtype": name, "gb_per_seq": round(per_seq / 1e9, 3), "max_concurrent": int(gpu_kv_gb * 1e9 / per_seq), }) return rows for r in kv_quantization_benefit(32, 8, 128, 8192): print(r) # {'dtype': 'fp16', 'gb_per_seq': 1.074, 'max_concurrent': 55} # {'dtype': 'fp8', 'gb_per_seq': 0.537, 'max_concurrent': 111} # {'dtype': 'int4', 'gb_per_seq': 0.268, 'max_concurrent': 223} ``` ```bash vllm serve meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct \ --kv-cache-dtype fp8_e5m2 \ --calculate-kv-scales ``` **FP8 KV cache is close to free.** Typical perplexity impact is under 0.1, and you get 2× the concurrency. On H100-class hardware with native FP8 support it is also faster. **INT4 KV cache needs care.** Quality degradation becomes measurable, especially on long contexts, and the standard mitigation is to keep the most recent tokens in higher precision — recent keys and values receive the most attention weight. **Always measure.** Run your evaluation suite with and without quantized KV; a two-point drop on a reasoning benchmark is not worth 2× concurrency for most products. ##### Speculative decoding The technique that attacks decode latency directly. The insight: decode is memory-bandwidth bound, so the GPU is mostly idle. **A small draft model proposes several tokens cheaply; the large model verifies them all in one forward pass** — the same cost as generating one token, because verification is a parallel prefill-like operation. ```mermaid flowchart LR A["Draft model
1B params"] -->|"proposes 4 tokens
~4ms total"| B["' the quick brown fox'"] B --> C["Target model
70B params"] C -->|"verifies all 4 in
ONE forward pass ~25ms"| D{"Accept?"} D -->|"3 accepted"| E["Emit 3 tokens
for the cost of 1"] D -->|"4th rejected"| F["Resample from
target distribution"] E --> A F --> A ``` **Crucially, the output distribution is unchanged.** Leviathan et al.'s rejection sampling scheme guarantees the generated text is distributed identically to what the target model alone would produce. This is a pure speedup, not an approximation. ```python import torch def speculative_step(draft_model, target_model, prefix_ids, gamma=4, temperature=1.0): """One speculative round. Returns accepted tokens.""" draft_tokens, draft_probs = [], [] cur = prefix_ids # 1. Draft gamma tokens autoregressively (cheap) for _ in range(gamma): logits = draft_model(cur).logits[:, -1, :] / temperature probs = torch.softmax(logits, dim=-1) tok = torch.multinomial(probs, 1) draft_tokens.append(tok) draft_probs.append(probs.gather(-1, tok)) cur = torch.cat([cur, tok], dim=-1) # 2. Target verifies ALL gamma in one forward pass target_logits = target_model(cur).logits[:, -gamma-1:-1, :] / temperature target_probs = torch.softmax(target_logits, dim=-1) # 3. Rejection sampling — preserves the target distribution exactly accepted = [] for i, tok in enumerate(draft_tokens): p_target = target_probs[:, i, :].gather(-1, tok) p_draft = draft_probs[i] r = torch.rand_like(p_target) if (r < (p_target / p_draft).clamp(max=1.0)).all(): accepted.append(tok) else: # Resample from the adjusted residual distribution residual = (target_probs[:, i, :] - draft_probs_full[i]).clamp(min=0) residual = residual / residual.sum(dim=-1, keepdim=True) accepted.append(torch.multinomial(residual, 1)) break return accepted, len(accepted) / gamma # tokens, acceptance rate ``` **The economics:** ```python def speculative_speedup(acceptance_rate, gamma, draft_cost_ratio=0.05): """Expected speedup from speculative decoding.""" # Expected accepted tokens per round (geometric until first rejection) a = acceptance_rate expected = (1 - a ** (gamma + 1)) / (1 - a) if a < 1 else gamma + 1 cost_per_round = 1 + gamma * draft_cost_ratio # 1 target + gamma draft return round(expected / cost_per_round, 2) for a in [0.5, 0.7, 0.8, 0.9]: for g in [3, 5, 8]: print(f"acceptance {a}, gamma {g}: {speculative_speedup(a, g)}× speedup") ``` **Acceptance rate is everything.** It depends on how well the draft model predicts the target's distribution: | Draft-target pair | Typical acceptance | Speedup | |---|---|---| | Llama-3-1B → Llama-3-70B | 0.75–0.85 | 2.0–2.8× | | Same family, distilled draft | 0.80–0.90 | 2.5–3.2× | | Unrelated small model | 0.40–0.55 | 1.2–1.5× | | n-gram / prompt lookup | 0.30–0.70 (task-dependent) | 1.3–2.5× | **Same-family drafts work best** because they were trained on similar data and have similar output distributions. ```bash # vLLM speculative decoding vllm serve meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-70B-Instruct \ --speculative-model meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct \ --num-speculative-tokens 5 \ --tensor-parallel-size 4 # n-gram speculation — no draft model, great for RAG and code vllm serve meta-llama/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct \ --speculative-model "[ngram]" \ --num-speculative-tokens 4 \ --ngram-prompt-lookup-max 4 ``` **N-gram speculation deserves attention for RAG.** It looks for the current n-gram in the prompt and proposes the continuation that followed it. When the model is quoting or lightly paraphrasing retrieved context — which is exactly what grounded RAG does — acceptance rates are very high and it costs nothing, since there is no draft model to run. **Medusa** takes a different approach: add several prediction heads to the target model itself, each predicting a token at a future position. No separate draft model, but it requires training the heads. Typical speedups are 2–3× with lower memory cost than a draft model. **When speculative decoding does not help:** at high batch sizes. Speculation trades extra compute for reduced memory traffic, and at large batches you are already compute-bound, so there is no idle capacity to exploit. It is a **latency** optimisation for low-to-medium concurrency, not a throughput one. ##### Measuring speculation ```python import time import numpy as np async def benchmark_speculation(base_url, model, prompts, max_tokens=256): """Compare with and without speculative decoding.""" from openai import AsyncOpenAI client = AsyncOpenAI(base_url=base_url, api_key="none") latencies, tpots, token_counts = [], [], [] for prompt in prompts: t0 = time.perf_counter() ttft = None n = 0 stream = await client.chat.completions.create( model=model, messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}], max_tokens=max_tokens, temperature=0.0, stream=True) async for chunk in stream: if chunk.choices and chunk.choices[0].delta.content: if ttft is None: ttft = time.perf_counter() - t0 n += 1 total = time.perf_counter() - t0 latencies.append(total) tpots.append((total - ttft) / max(n - 1, 1)) token_counts.append(n) return { "mean_e2e_s": round(float(np.mean(latencies)), 2), "mean_tpot_ms": round(float(np.mean(tpots)) * 1000, 2), "tokens_per_s": round(float(np.mean(token_counts)) / float(np.mean(latencies)), 1), } ``` Query vLLM's metrics endpoint for the acceptance rate: ```bash curl http://localhost:8000/metrics | grep spec_decode # vllm:spec_decode_num_accepted_tokens_total # vllm:spec_decode_num_draft_tokens_total # vllm:spec_decode_draft_acceptance_rate ``` **If acceptance is below 0.6, the draft model is a poor match** — try a smaller `gamma`, a same-family draft, or n-gram speculation instead. ##### Bounding KV memory The assignment. Four levers, in order of preference. **1. Reduce `max_model_len`** to your actual maximum. Free, and it directly raises achievable concurrency. **2. Quantize the cache** to FP8. Near-free, 2× concurrency. **3. Cap concurrency** with `max_num_seqs` so you never exceed the budget. **4. Enable swapping and preemption** as a safety valve: ```bash vllm serve ... --swap-space 8 --preemption-mode swap ``` vLLM preempts by either recomputing (cheap for short sequences) or swapping to CPU (better for long ones). Both cost latency, so treat preemption as a backstop rather than a plan. **Attention-window techniques** bound the cache structurally: | Technique | Mechanism | Trade-off | |---|---|---| | Sliding window (Mistral) | Attend only to the last W tokens | Info propagates across layers; some loss | | StreamingLLM | Keep 4 "attention sink" tokens + recent window | Enables infinite streaming | | H2O | Evict tokens with low cumulative attention | Task-dependent quality impact | | SnapKV | Compress the prompt's KV at prefill | Good for long-prompt, short-output | **Attention sinks are a genuinely surprising finding.** Xiao et al. showed that the first few tokens accumulate large attention weight regardless of their content — they act as a "no-op" destination for attention mass. Evicting them causes a dramatic quality collapse; keeping just four alongside a sliding window enables stable generation over unbounded streams. ##### Common mistakes - **Variable content at the start of the prompt**, destroying prefix cache hits — the timestamp problem. - **Prefix caching disabled** with a long fixed system prompt. - **Not verifying `cache_read_input_tokens`** and assuming caching is working. - **`max_model_len` far above real usage**, wasting KV budget. - **INT4 KV cache without evaluating quality.** - **Speculative decoding at high batch sizes**, where there is no idle capacity to exploit. - **An unrelated draft model** with an acceptance rate below 0.6. - **`gamma` too large** — rejected tokens waste draft compute, and 4–6 is usually optimal. - **Ignoring n-gram speculation for RAG**, where it is free and highly effective. - **Evicting attention-sink tokens** in a sliding-window scheme. - **Treating preemption as normal** rather than as a signal that concurrency is over-provisioned. ##### Hands-on: enable both, measure both Your practical task enables prefix caching and speculative decoding and measures latency reduction. Test them separately before combining, because they improve different phases — prefix caching cuts TTFT, speculation cuts TPOT. Use a workload with a long fixed system prompt for the first and short prompts with long outputs for the second, so each optimisation is exercised where it matters. The mini project benchmarks speculative decoding across draft models and quantifies the acceptance rate. Try three drafts: a same-family small model, an unrelated small model, and n-gram. Plot acceptance rate against speedup and confirm the relationship matches the `speculative_speedup` formula. Then re-run at batch size 32 and watch the speedup collapse — that is the compute-bound regime, and seeing it directly is the lesson. The assignment analyses KV cache scaling with context and batch, and strategies to bound it. Build the table for your own model showing GB per sequence at several context lengths, the resulting max concurrency on your GPU, and how each of the four levers changes it. Close with a recommended configuration for a specific latency and concurrency target, with the arithmetic shown. ##### Key takeaways - **The KV cache scales linearly with both context length and batch size**, which makes it the binding constraint on the two things you most want to increase. - **Prefix caching is nearly free and often the largest TTFT win** — put stable content first and variable content last, then verify your hit rate. - **FP8 KV quantization doubles concurrency for negligible quality cost**; INT4 needs evaluation. - **Speculative decoding is exact, not approximate** — rejection sampling preserves the target distribution — and it is a latency optimisation that stops helping at high batch sizes. - **Acceptance rate determines the speedup.** Use a same-family draft, keep `gamma` around 4–6, and reach for n-gram speculation on RAG workloads where the model is quoting retrieved text.
practical_task_reference: Enable prefix caching and speculative decoding in a serving engine and measure latency reduction.
mini_project_reference: Benchmark speculative decoding with different draft models and quantify the accepted-token rate and speedup.
